danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 19
paragraphs: Ved herrernes ende af bordet blev samtalen livligere og livligere. Obersten fortalte dem, at krigserklæringen allerede var udkommet i Petersborg, og at en kopi, som han selv havde set, var blevet sendt med kurer til øverstkommanderende den dag.
»Og hvorfor pokker skal vi kæmpe mod Bonaparte?« bemærkede Sjinsjin. »Han har lukket munden på Østrig, og jeg er bange for, det bliver vores tur nu.«
Obersten var en svær, høj, rødmosset tysker, tydeligvis hengiven til tjenesten og patriotisk russisk. Han ærgrede sig over Sjinsjins bemærkning.

»Det er af den grund, min gode herre,« sagde han og talte med tysk accent, »af den grund, at kejseren ved det. Han erklærer i manifestet, at han ikke kan se med ligegyldighed på den fare, der truer Rusland, og at rigets sikkerhed og værdighed samt dets alliances hellighed...« han betonede dette sidste ord med særlig eftertryk, som om netop deri lå sagens kerne.
Derpå gentog han med den fejlfri embedshukommelse, der kendetegnede ham, manifestets indledningsord:

... og ønsket, som udgør kejserens eneste og absolutte mål — at grundfæste freden i Europa på fast grundlag — har nu bestemt ham til at sende en del af hæren til udlandet og skabe nye betingelser for opnåelsen af dette mål.
»Derfor, min kære herre, er det sådan,« sluttede han, drak et glas vin med værdighed og kiggede hen på greven for at få hans bifald.

»Kender De ordsproget: 'Jansen, Jansen, bliv nu hjemme og drejs dine tene!'?« sagde Sjinsjin, rynkede brynene og smilede. »Cela nous convient à merveille. Suvorov forstod nu, hvad han lavede; og alligevel slog de ham à plate couture — og hvor finder vi en Suvorov nu? Je vous demande un peu,« sagde han og skiftede ustandseligt mellem fransk og russisk.
Kender De ordsproget?
Det passer os aldeles udmærket.
Helt og aldeles.
Det spørger jeg bare om.

»Vi må kæmpe til den sidste dr-r-råbe af vores blod!« sagde obersten og hamrede i bordet; »og vi må dø for vores kejser, og så bliver alt godt. Og vi skal drøfte det så lidt som mu-u-uligt« — han dvælede særligt ved ordet muligt — »så lidt som mu-u-uligt,« sluttede han og vendte sig atter mod greven. »Det er, hvad vi gamle husarer mener, og dermed basta! Og hvad mener De, unge mand og unge husar, hvad mener De om det?« tilføjede han henvendt til Nikolaj, der, da han hørte, at der blev talt om krig, havde vendt sig fra sin borddame med øjne og ører spidset mod obersten.

»Jeg er helt enig med Dem,« svarede Nikolaj, blussede op, drejede sin tallerken rundt og flyttede rundt på sine vinglas med lige så megen beslutsomhed og desperation, som om han i dette øjeblik stod over for en stor fare. »Jeg er overbevist om, at vi russere enten må dø eller sejre,« sluttede han, bevidst — som andre også var — om at hans bemærkning efter at være udtalt var for entusiastisk og emfatisk til lejligheden og derfor malplaceret.
»Det, De lige sagde, var glimrende!« sagde hans borddame Julie.
Sonja sitrede over hele kroppen og rødmede til ørerne og bag dem og ned over hals og skuldre, mens Nikolaj talte.
Pierre lyttede til oberstens tale og nikkede bifaldende.
»Det er udmærket,« sagde han.
»Det unge menneske er en ægte husar!« råbte obersten og hamrede atter i bordet.

»Hvad er det for en larm derovre?« lød Marja Dmitrijevnas dybe stemme pludselig fra den anden ende af bordet. »Hvad hamrer du i bordet for?« spurgte hun obersten. »Og hvorfor hidser du dig op? Tror du, franskmændene er her?«
»Jeg taler sandhed,« svarede husaren med et smil.
»Det handler om krigen,« råbte greven ned langs bordet. »Du ved, min søn skal af sted, Marja Dmitrijevna? Min søn skal af sted.«

»Jeg har fire sønner i hæren, og alligevel jammer jeg ikke. Det ligger alt sammen i Guds hænder. Man kan dø i sin seng, eller Gud kan spare én i et slag,« svarede Marja Dmitrijevnas dybe stemme, der ubesværet bar hele bordets længde.
»Det er sandt!«
Endnu engang samledes samtalerne — damernes i den ene ende og herrernes i den anden.
»Du tør ikke spørge,« sagde Natasjas lillebror; »det ved jeg, du tør ikke!«
»Jo, det tør jeg,« svarede Natasja.
Hendes ansigt blussede pludselig af hensynsløs og glad beslutsomhed. Hun rejste sig halvt, indbød med et blik Pierre, der sad over for hende, til at lytte til det, der kom, og vendte sig mod sin mor:
»Mamma!« klang hendes barnlige stemmes klare kontraalttoner, hørlige hele bordets længde.
»Hvad er det?« spurgte grevinden forskrækket; men da hun af sin datters ansigt kunne se, at det kun var drillerier, rystede hun advarende og formanende en finger ad hende.
Samtalen forstummede.
»Mamma! Hvad skal vi have af sødt?« Og Natasjas stemme lød endnu fastere og mere beslutsom.
Grevinden forsøgte at se streng ud, men kunne ikke. Marja Dmitrijevna rystede sin tykke finger.
»Kosakpige!« sagde hun truende.
De fleste af gæsterne, der var usikre på, hvordan de skulle opfatte dette udbrud, kiggede på de ældre.
»Du skal bare passe på!« sagde grevinden.
»Mamma! Hvad skal vi have af sødt?« råbte Natasja atter dristigt, med fræk munterhed, sikker på at hendes streg ville blive taget i god mening.
Sonja og den tykke lille Petja bøjede sig dobbelt af latter.
»Kan du se! Jeg spurgte,« hviskede Natasja til sin lillebror og til Pierre og skævede til ham igen.
»Ispudding, men du får ingen,« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna.
Natasja indså, at der ikke var noget at være bange for, og trodsede selv Marja Dmitrijevna.
»Marja Dmitrijevna! Hvad for en slags ispudding? Jeg kan ikke lide flødeis.«
»Gulerodsis.«
»Nej! Hvad for en slags, Marja Dmitrijevna? Hvad for en slags?« næsten skreg hun; »jeg vil vide det!«

Marja Dmitrijevna og grevinden brast i latter, og alle gæsterne stemte i. Alle lo, ikke af Marja Dmitrijevnas svar, men af den utrolige dristighed og snuhed hos denne lille pige, der havde vovet at behandle Marja Dmitrijevna på den måde.

Natasja gav først op, da hun havde fået at vide, at der ville være ananasis. Før isen blev champagne serveret rundt. Orkestret spillede igen op, greven og grevinden kyssede hinanden, og gæsterne rejste sig fra deres pladser for at 'lykønske' grevinden og rakte hen over bordet for at klinke glas med greven, med børnene og med hinanden. Atter myldrede lakajerne rundt, stole skrabede, og i samme rækkefølge, som de var kommet ind, men med rødere ansigter, vendte gæsterne tilbage til dagligstuen og grevens kontor.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: At the men's end of the table the conversation grew more and more animated. The colonel told them that the declaration of war had already appeared in Petersburg and that a copy, which he had seen with his own eyes, had been sent that very day by courier to the commander in chief.
"And why the hell are we going to fight Bonaparte?" Shinshin remarked. "He's already shut Austria up, and I'm afraid we're next."
The colonel was a stout, tall, red-faced German, clearly devoted to the military and patriotically Russian. He took offense at Shinshin's comment.

"It is because, my good sir," he said, speaking with a heavy German accent, "because ze Emperor knows zat. He says in ze manifesto zat he cannot look wiz indifference at ze danger zreatening Russia, and zat ze safety and dignity of ze Empire, as well as ze sanctity of its alliances..." He emphasized this last word as if it contained the whole point of the matter.
Then, with the flawless official memory that characterized him, he recited the opening words of the manifesto:

...and the wish, which constitutes the Emperor's sole and absolute aim—to establish peace in Europe on firm foundations—has now decided him to dispatch part of the army abroad and to create a new condition for the attainment of that purpose.
"Zat, my dear sir, is vy..." he concluded, drinking a glass of wine with dignity and looking to the count for approval.

[Speaking in French] "Do you know the proverb: 'Jerome, Jerome, don't roam—stay home and turn your spindles'?" said Shinshin, wrinkling his brow and smiling. [Speaking in French] "That suits us perfectly. Suvorov, now—he knew what he was doing, and even he was beaten to a pulp. And where are we going to find a Suvorov today? [Speaking in French] I ask you." He kept switching between French and Russian.
* Do you know the proverb?
* (2) That suits us down to the ground.
* (3) Hollow.
* (4) I just ask you that.

"Ve must fight to the last d-d-drop of our blood!" the colonel shouted, thumping the table. "And ve must die for our Emperor, and zen all vill be vell. And ve must discuss it as little as p-p-possible"—he lingered on the word—"as p-p-possible," he repeated, turning once more to the count. "Zat is how ve old hussars see it, and zere's an end of it! And how do you, a young man and a young hussar—how do you see it?" he added, turning to Nicholas, who had swiveled away from his dinner partner the moment he heard the war being discussed, all eyes and ears on the colonel.

"I completely agree with you," Nicholas replied, flaring up. He turned his plate around and shifted his wineglasses about with the same decisiveness and desperation as if he were facing mortal danger at that very moment. "I am convinced that we Russians must die or conquer," he concluded—aware, as was everyone else, that his words had come out too passionate and dramatic for the occasion and were therefore awkward.
"What you just said was splendid!" said his dinner partner Julie.
Sonya trembled from head to toe and blushed to her ears, behind her ears, and all the way down her neck and shoulders while Nicholas was speaking.
Pierre had been listening to the colonel's speech and nodding in agreement.
"That's fine," he said.
"The young man's a true hussar!" shouted the colonel, thumping the table again.

"What's all that racket down there?" Marya Dmitrievna's deep voice suddenly demanded from the other end of the table. "What are you banging the table for?" she said to the hussar. "And why are you getting so worked up? Do you think the French are here?"
"I am speaking ze truce," the hussar replied with a smile.
"It's all about the war," the count called down the table. "You know my son is going, Marya Dmitrievna? My son is going."

"I have four sons in the army, but I don't sit here worrying. It's all in God's hands. You can die in your bed, or God may spare you on the battlefield," Marya Dmitrievna replied in her deep voice, which carried easily the full length of the table.
"That's true!"
Once again the conversation split in two—the ladies' at one end, the men's at the other.
"You won't ask," Natasha's little brother was saying. "I know you won't ask!"
"I will," replied Natasha.
Her face suddenly flushed with reckless, joyous determination. She half rose, caught Pierre's eye across the table to make sure he was watching what was coming, and turned to her mother.
"Mama!" rang out the clear contralto of her childish voice, audible the whole length of the table.
"What is it?" asked the countess, startled. But seeing from her daughter's face that it was only mischief, she wagged a stern, threatening finger at her.
The conversation died down.
"Mama! What sweets are we going to have?" Natasha's voice sounded even firmer and more resolute now.
The countess tried to frown but couldn't manage it. Marya Dmitrievna shook her thick finger.
"Cossack!" she said threateningly.
Most of the guests, unsure how to react to this outburst, looked at the elders.
"You'd better watch yourself!" said the countess.
"Mama! What sweets are we going to have?" Natasha cried again, boldly, with cheeky delight, confident her prank would be taken in good humor.
Sonya and chubby little Petya doubled over with laughter.
"You see? I asked," Natasha whispered to her little brother and to Pierre, glancing at him again.
"Ice pudding—but you won't get any," said Marya Dmitrievna.
Natasha saw there was nothing to be afraid of and decided to take on even Marya Dmitrievna.
"Marya Dmitrievna! What kind of ice pudding? I don't like ice cream."
"Carrot ices."
"No! What kind, Marya Dmitrievna? What kind?" she practically screamed. "I want to know!"

Marya Dmitrievna and the countess burst out laughing, and all the guests joined in. Everyone laughed not at Marya Dmitrievna's answer but at the unbelievable boldness and spunk of this little girl who had dared to challenge Marya Dmitrievna like that.

Natasha only gave up when she'd been told there would be pineapple ice cream. Before the ices, champagne was served. The band struck up again, the count and countess kissed, and the guests rose from their seats to "congratulate" the countess, reaching across the table to clink glasses with the count, the children, and one another. Once more the footmen rushed about, chairs scraped, and in the same order as they had entered—but with redder faces—the guests filed back into the drawing room and the count's study.
